direction.comments: The direction on a macroscale feels very Danny Boyle, as he goes back to his old roots with a fast-paced movie that's super punk rock in a very British way; the direction on a microscale is strong, carried a lot by good performances and very sharp dialogue, which is really what makes the movie, and you can tell it's based on a play because the script and acting come together to tell a very interesting story that's kind of emblematic of clickbait, all about keeping your attention in a very unethical way; the storytelling is good, showing the rise of this punk, fast-paced, unethical company and how it keeps pushing the envelope despite going against ethics and what's right, and while it takes a bit of a hit during the kidnapping arc, it picks back up in the climax when they decide to put nudity in the paper; the tension is built very well, as you're so locked into what's going on with these characters that you really want to see how everything plays out for The Sun, especially as they keep breaking barriers and doing unethical things to get ahead

performance.comments: Carries the movie very well, showing how corrupted his character gets as he starts working for the paper to spite the people who wronged him, only to create a monster and become one himself because he's so power-hungry and obsessed with being number one, a transition he shows very well, and his really good chemistry with Claire Foy and Guy Pearce helps him carry it on his shoulders

Gives a very good performance that I very much enjoyed, and while I don't think it deserves an Oscar nomination, it shows why he deserved one for The Brutalist, as he transforms into Rupert Murdoch, a guy who says he's about ethics but actually just cares about money and will turn a blind eye as long as it pays; he also shows a good range of emotions, from power to anger, and his dynamic with Jack O'Connell is good and helps make the movie

Plays her character well and does a good job with the material she's given, as her character is probably the most ethical person at a company full of unethical people, yet she still isn't ethical either; she also has a good dynamic with Jack O'Connell, and I very much enjoyed her performance

cast.comments: Everyone plays their role well with no bad performances, bringing forth this punk rock, fast-paced, somewhat comedic British cast of characters that helps drive the story forward and show how much of an impact The Sun has on society, and they cast it well

story.comments: The concept is based on James Graham's play about the origins of The Sun and how it sensationalized the news and basically created tabloid culture, starting with Rupert Murdoch buying the paper to turn it into a tabloid and the unethical things they begin doing to get the reader's attention; the plot structure is good but flawed, as the first half sets up the exposition well with The Sun doing whatever it takes to become number one, but the kidnapping that takes up the first 20 to 30 minutes of the second half is very poor, since The Sun's side of it is handled well but the actual kidnapping is executed poorly, and while it turns back around in the climax, the resolution is so stupid that it legitimately ruins the movie, between a few seconds of AI that feel like an investor play and a tacky final shot sequence that mixes the ending of Babylon with an attempt at an Oppenheimer moment; character writing is very good, as you see the motivations of all the characters, from Rupert Murdoch, who the movie sympathizes with to an extent while showing he's not the moral man he thinks he is, to Larry Lamb, whose quest for revenge on the people who wronged him at the Daily Mirror cascades into him being corrupted by power and creating a monster, to Claire Foy's character, who's somewhat of a moral figure but still corrupt herself, which shows how a lot of corrupt individuals come together to create this dishonest monster, and I really enjoyed these characters and wish I got to see more of them

screenplay.comments: The dialogue is so sharp, flows very well, and is very profound, and it's obvious it came from an award-winning play since it feels so much like one, giving the actors material to work with to create really interesting conversations; the humor is injected throughout to make it feel like a very punk rock, rowdy environment, even if it's not a super funny movie; the symbolism is very strong, with an Oppenheimer-type message of 'look at the monster we created,' as the creation of The Sun and its push far past journalistic ethics show how society ended up with the truly unethical, sensationalized news we have today, and it shows how corrupted these people get with power, from Rupert Murdoch, a hypocrite who says they're going too far but keeps turning a blind eye because it's so successful despite having so many chances to step in and say no, to Larry Lamb, who sets out to one-up the people who wronged him but gets so lost in it that he becomes a monster, and while it gets a little overt and tacky by the end, it's still profound and shares its message on such a pertinent topic very well; the foreshadowing is mostly there to set up the climax, with a moment 20 to 30 minutes in that does a good job showing the direction The Sun is going

soundtrack.comments: Helps transport you to the time period, and make the film feel very british punk

cinematography.comments: Shot like an old-school Danny Boyle movie mixed with some of his newer techniques, as he shoots it like a punk rock movie with a lot of cool, unique shots, from the Dutch angles, which I don't see movies do a lot, to the fast-moving shots, but he also does these tacky slow-motion and iPhone-style shots that look so bad, and while that's very Danny Boyle, I really don't like it when he does that

editing.comments: Very punk rock and in your face, with a lot of cool techniques, like the filter at the beginning and the overlays throughout, and its fast-paced, hip-hop-style edits add to the Danny Boyle flavor, though it also makes his annoying shots even tackier, and I'd be really interested to know what role AI played in the editing

visual_effects.comments: This is where we all have to have the conversation about this movie; there are a lot of cool visuals, like the fast-moving paper printing, the overlays, and the filter at the beginning, while the train sequences are a little tacky, and I wouldn't be surprised if those used AI; the AI mice honestly didn't bother me since they just look like regular VFX and add what they need to, but the few seconds of AI in the transition from the climax to the resolution are poorly done, forced in, and add absolutely nothing, so cutting them would leave the exact same movie, and one key credit makes it very obvious they were added because of the investors; since they used it there, I have a feeling they used AI in other places they didn't announce, as some of the tackier visuals might be AI

production_design.comments: Really good, as it transports you to a late-1960s London newspaper room and throughout London in that time period, which they capture very well, and the printing press is really cool, with sequences I very much enjoyed that add to the punk rock, fast-paced style of the movie

makeup.comments: Does a pretty good job transporting you to the late 1960s

costumes.comments: Does a pretty good job transporting you to the late 1960s

review.pacing: The right pacing for the most part, except for the kidnapping sequence, which I get is important for the newspaper but isn't well executed, feels a little forced, and goes on a little too long, so cutting it in half would shave off about 10 minutes and make the movie an hour and 45 minutes long, which feels fair
review.climax: Picks the movie back up after the kidnapping sequence and ends it right, showing the key moment in the newspaper's history where they go past the point of no return and the impact it has on the paper, and it's executed very well in a very punk rock way that shows them breaking journalistic ethics and only caring about the numbers; beyond the AI, the resolution has one well-acted scene that's actually good and would have ended the movie well, but then the final shot sequence is legitimately like the ending of Babylon, and while I get why they do it, since it shows the Oppenheimer-like domino effect The Sun had on the culture by making people care more about telling a story than reporting the right one because there's more money in keeping people engaged, it puts way too much on screen way too fast to read everything, so I didn't like it that much
review.tone: Very traditional Danny Boyle, as this punk rock, fast-paced '60s movie feels like his Wolf of Wall Street with its British take on an unethical company, and to an extent like his Oppenheimer with its symbolism
review.final_notes: Saw a screening at Austin Film Festival; the use of AI in this movie legitimately feels like it was only there to appease investors, as it adds no value to the movie
review.overall: Overall, 'Ink' is a very well-made, sharply written movie that I really enjoyed despite a lot of flaws, as it's carried by good performances and shows how The Sun sensationalized the news and created a monster that ended up changing the world, making it feel like Danny Boyle's Oppenheimer moment; even the AI, which very much feels like it came from the investors, is symbolic of the movie itself, as the filmmakers were willing to turn a blind eye to the ethics of including it for the money in order to tell the story they wanted to tell, just like The Sun
